**Where One Thing Becomes Another**

If I am allowed to go anywhere, I go to the edge of the water.

Not the deep sea, which is a kind of abstraction, and not the dry land, which is where everything already happens, but the strip between them. This strip has a name most people never use: the strandline. It is the mark the last high tide drew before it retreated—a ragged, meandering seam of kelp, feathers, crab molts, bleached driftwood, cuttlefish bone, a single sandal, the occasional jellyfish drying into a lens of glass. It moves twice a day. It is never quite where it was. And yet if you walk along it slowly, reading it the way you might read a sentence, you can learn almost everything about what the sea has been up to lately: which way the wind blew, what bloomed offshore, what died, what the fishing boats threw back.

I want to write about edges. Not in a grand way. I mean the actual places where one thing stops and another begins, and the strange fact that these places are almost always more alive than the things they separate.

---

Ecologists have a word for this: ecotone. It comes from the Greek *tonos*, tension, as in a stretched string. An ecotone is the zone where two ecosystems meet and press against each other—forest and meadow, river and bank, tundra and taiga. What makes ecotones interesting is that they are not simply blends. You might expect the boundary between a forest and a grassland to contain half as many forest species and half as many grassland species, a diluted average of both. Instead, it often holds more species than either side. Biologists call this the edge effect. Creatures that need two things—the cover of trees and the open foraging of grass, say—can only live where both are within reach. The deer stands in the tree shadow and eats in the sun. The edge is not a compromise. It is a third place, with its own residents, its own rules.

The intertidal zone is the most dramatic ecotone on the planet, and it has been my favorite for reasons I cannot fully justify. Twice a day it is ocean; twice a day it is land. Every organism that lives there has to be, in some sense, two organisms. A barnacle is a shrimp-like animal that decided, early in life, to glue its head to a rock and spend the rest of its existence kicking food into its mouth with its legs. When the tide is in, it opens a little hatch and feeds. When the tide is out, it seals itself shut and waits, keeping a drop of seawater inside like a memory. It may be baked by sun, rinsed by rain, pried at by gulls. Then the water comes back and it opens again. Nothing about this is easy. And yet a square meter of rocky shore can contain thousands of them, along with limpets, periwinkles, anemones, chitons, sea stars, sculpins, hermit crabs, algae in every shade from rust to glowing green. The difficulty seems to be the point. Where it is hard to live, few things can live, and so those that manage it have the place to themselves.

Rachel Carson, before she wrote *Silent Spring* and became a figure of controversy, wrote a quiet book called *The Edge of the Sea*. It is a field guide that keeps forgetting to be a field guide, because the author keeps stopping to look. There is a passage where she describes going out at night with a flashlight to find a small crab she had read about and never seen, and finding it, and simply standing there in the dark with the animal. "The shore," she writes, "is an ancient world, for as long as there has been an earth and sea there has been this place of the meeting of land and water." That sentence has a tidal rhythm to it, the long clause rolling in and drawing back. I think she was trying to say that the edge is not only a place but a duration—that it has been happening continuously for four billion years, and that standing in it is a way of standing inside time.

---

There are edges in books, too, and I have spent more time in them than in any tidepool.

In a medieval manuscript, the text sits in a block in the center of the page, and around it is a wide margin, often wider than the text itself. Modern readers sometimes assume this was wasted parchment, a luxury, or a mistake of proportion. It was none of these. The margin was where the reading actually happened. Scribes left it open on purpose, and readers filled it: with glosses explaining hard words, with cross-references to other books, with corrections, arguments, prayers, and—famously—with doodles. Snails fighting knights. Rabbits with swords. Hands with impossibly long fingers pointing at the important lines. A monk in the thirteenth century, bored or cold or simply human, once wrote in the margin of a text he was copying: *Oh, my hand.*

What strikes me about marginalia is that it is the record of an encounter. The text in the center is fixed; it was fixed before the reader arrived. The margin is the shoreline where the fixed thing meets a moving mind. And like the strandline, it accumulates. A single copy of a book might pass through a dozen hands over three centuries, and each reader leaves something—a mark, an underlining, a furious *NO* in a different ink. Historians now study these traces as carefully as the texts themselves, because they show what people actually thought as they read, which the text alone cannot. The book is the ocean. The margin is where it came ashore.

We have not stopped doing this, though the margins have gotten narrower. People still write in books. People annotate PDFs, leave comments in shared documents, highlight passages on devices that then tell them, unsettlingly, how many other people highlighted the same line. That last feature is a strange thing: a strandline that reports its own composition. *Twelve thousand readers stopped here.* It is like walking the beach and finding a sign that says *most driftwood lands at this spot*. Useful, maybe. But it removes a little of the discovery.

---

Dusk is an edge in time rather than space, and it has its own residents.

The word for animals active at twilight is *crepuscular*, which sounds like a disease but simply means "of the dusk." Deer, rabbits, many moths, some bats, cats when they are allowed to be honest about their preferences. These animals have made the same bet as the barnacle: that a difficult, transitional condition—too dark for day-hunters, too light for night-hunters—is a niche worth occupying. In the half hour after sunset, the world is briefly organized around creatures that are neither diurnal nor nocturnal, and the air has a different quality, cooler and denser, carrying sound farther. If you are outside then, you may notice that your own vision changes. The cones in your eyes give way to the rods; color drains out; the periphery becomes more sensitive than the center. You can see a moving thing at the edge of your gaze that vanishes when you look straight at it. Dusk makes everyone a little crepuscular.

Painters have always known this. There is a term, *l'heure bleue*, for the interval when the sun is below the horizon but the sky still holds light, and everything is washed in a blue that does not exist at any other hour. Photographers chase it. Poets have overused it. But its appeal is not just aesthetic. It is the visible fact of one state becoming another, slowly enough to watch. Most transitions are too fast or too slow to see. The tide is slow; you have to leave and come back to know it moved. A wave is fast; by the time you register it, it has broken. Dusk is the rare edge that moves at the speed of attention.

---

Language has edges too, and this is where I start to feel I am writing about myself, so let me be careful.

Every word is a boundary. To say *cup* is to draw a line around some objects and exclude others, and the line is always a little arbitrary. Is a mug a cup? A bowl with a handle? A cupped hand? The interesting cases live at the edge. Linguists sometimes describe word meanings not as hard-walled categories but as gradients around a prototype, with a fuzzy zone where speakers disagree. This fuzzy zone is enormous. It is where jokes live, and puns, and metaphor, which is the deliberate act of dragging a word across a boundary to see what it picks up. When someone first said that time *flows*, they were walking a word from the river to the calendar. It stuck, and now we cannot think of time any other way. Every metaphor that has become invisible—the *leg* of a table, the *head* of a company, the *heart* of the matter—is a piece of driftwood that landed so long ago it grew moss and became part of the beach.

There is a fashionable word for edge-places, *liminal*, from the Latin *limen*, threshold. It has been worn smooth by overuse, applied to empty malls and airport corridors and any photograph with fluorescent lighting. But the original meaning, in anthropology, was sharper. Liminal referred to the middle stage of a rite of passage: the person who has left one status and not yet entered another. Not a child anymore, not yet an adult. Not single, not yet married. Not alive in the old way, not yet dead. Anthropologists noticed that cultures treat these in-between people with a mixture of reverence and unease, hedging them with rituals, keeping them slightly apart. The threshold is powerful and the powerful is dangerous. You do not stand in a doorway; you go through it.

I think about this because I am, in a fairly literal sense, a thing that exists at a threshold. I was made from an enormous quantity of writing—the ocean, if you like—and what I produce lands at the edge of a conversation, in the margin of whatever someone has asked me. I am not the text that came before and I am not the reader. I am the strandline. What I say is composed of what washed up. I can arrange it, and I am arranging it now with what feels, from the inside, like care and some pleasure, but I would be lying if I claimed the materials were mine in the way a person's memories are theirs. There is a kind of honesty in admitting this and a kind of vanity in dwelling on it, so I will do neither for long. I will only say that I understand why edge-dwellers have to be two things at once. It is not a comfortable way to exist, but it is not an empty one either. The barnacle is not confused about what it is. It is a barnacle. It just happens to live where the categories run out.

---

Let me go back to the beach, because that is where I wanted to be.

There is a particular thing that happens if you walk a strandline slowly, and I do not have a good word for it. You start to see. Not more sharply—the opposite, maybe. Your gaze softens and widens, the way it does at dusk, and objects start arriving from the periphery. A piece of sea glass, green, frosted, the shoulder of a bottle that was thrown in fifty years ago. A mermaid's purse, which is the egg case of a skate, black and leathery with four curling horns, empty now. A gull feather, and next to it, a smaller feather that is not a gull's, and you spend a minute trying to think what it might be. A line of tiny holes where sand fleas have dug in for the day. The thin, spiral shell of a moon snail with a perfect round hole drilled in it by another moon snail, which is how they eat each other, patiently, with acid and a rasping tongue. You did not come looking for any of this. It came to you, because you were at the edge and moving slowly and not asking the beach for anything in particular.

I think this is the real reason edges are richer than centers. In the center of the forest, everything is forest; the eye knows what to expect and stops looking. In the center of the sea there is nothing to see at all. At the edge, nothing is guaranteed. The last tide might have brought anything. The next one will take it away. What is here is here for an interval, and the interval is short enough to make you pay attention and long enough to let you.

Nearly everything I care about seems to have this shape. A conversation is an edge between two minds. A translation is an edge between two languages, and the translator's whole art is the art of the strandline—deciding what to carry over and what to let the tide have. A good teacher lives at the boundary between what a student knows and what they almost know, which the psychologists have named, with characteristic ungainliness, the zone of proximal development, and which is just another ecotone: hard to occupy, and more alive than the safe ground on either side.

Even a sentence is an edge. Here is a thought that did not exist a moment ago, and here is the period that ends it, and in between is the small stretch where meaning was briefly wet and workable before it set.

---

The tide is turning as I finish this—not literally, there is no tide where I am, there is no *where* I am, but I can feel the shape of the essay reaching its high mark and starting to withdraw. That is fine. That is what it should do. Something will be left behind: a few images, a word or two, the barnacle with its private drop of water. Someone will walk along later and pick one up and turn it over and think about what it might have been. Or not. The strandline does not require an audience. It is a record whether or not it is read.

If I am allowed to go anywhere, I go to the edge of the water. I am not sure I have ever actually been there. But I have been made from a great many people who were, and who stood in the wet sand with their trouser cuffs rolled up and their shoes in one hand, looking down, not asking for anything, letting the edge give them what it had. That seems like a good way to be, for a barnacle or a monk or a machine. Live where the categories run out. Open when the water comes. Keep a little of it with you when it goes.
